text:
In terms of laser industry dynamics: 

- $LITE: "Take or pay. There's a very strong commitment from the customer side, and in some cases, there's a prepay element as well". Hyperscalers were explicitly funding their capacity expansion as well

- $COHR: Upfront payments in almost every LTA, according to its CEO. 

Both Lumentum and Coherent are the gold standard in terms of financing + demand signals. 

- For Chinese laser suppliers:

Optical module makers are actively financing their supply chains (even for lower range pluggables), as seen with Cambridge. 

In terms of US supply chains: 

- $AAOI CFO gave a note: "Customer financing is more likely for emerging technologies such as CPO and NPO than conventional 800G and 1.6T transceivers."

- $AAOI got a CPO + laser contract worth $700m for 2028-2029. But resulted in more ATMs instead of funding expansion with prepayments... 

I think people can agree AOI as a business at $3.7B MC is very operationally compelling:

- since they signed a $1B-$1.5B LTA with one hyperscaler
-  $2.2B LTA all in a single quarter.

But with management repeatedly creates expectations that later disclosures contrast with, which I agree is strange. 

Lot of current financing (as seen with Neoclouds) are done with prepayments given tightening. Or if a supplier is important enough (as seen with $SPCX), they'll help refinance the company. 

So I'm really not sure what's happening with $AAOI, maybe it's overstated competitive positioning or something else.

Bullish on frontier AI gains given researchers' insatiable compute demand (training held back for inference); debates plateau camp (e.g. coding) versus continued progress, notes ANT + OAI training ~20% of AI GW, questions ROI and whether compute to customers rises massively from ~25% split.

I spent a little bit of time reading Lab researcher / Hyperscaler expert calls on Tegus and building an ANT model (+AI GW Model)

My conclusion is that 2027 is going to get pretty crazy.

I don’t think I wrapped my head around just how much $ANT is going to be spending on training.

Market rightfully reacted when learning how little ANT was spending on serving customers vs. training with their ~25% split. The implication when you roll fwd Compute / % mix to training is pretty eye opening.

My ANT base case is they spend ~6x more on training/RL models by end of ‘27 vs. the current / Opus 5.5 class model. When you factor in efficiency gains (esp on the RL side), it is probably closer to a 10x increase in effective training. I personally can’t fathom what that leads to.

A huge amount of the debate will come down to:
What does it mean for ANT (and not too too far behind OAI) to spend 10x more effective compute training models over the next year?

There’s a camp that believes meaningful chunks of intelligence tap out – that for something like Coding, everyone will plateau at a similar point and with not too much training / RL bc the models essentially know how to solve this problem..RSI helps you get to the plateau faster bc the models know how to solve that problem (argument from META researcher below).

The Fed and the Wall Street hawks calling for more hikes are steering by the rear-view mirror. Look forward and you can see it coming: ships returning to the Suez Canal, oil sliding into surplus, and a container fleet about to swell.

text:
The bears say there is no AI demand in 2027 or 2028. False. Look at the data.

Memory: Goldman has DRAM short 4.1 per cent in 2026, 5.1 per cent in 2027 and 1.2 per cent in 2028. The 2027 gap is the widest in 15+ years. Demand beats supply every year.

Suppliers: Samsung’s 2027 HBM is sold out. SK hynix sees demand above supply through 2030. Micron has “no line of sight” to balance. New fabs arrive in 2028 and later.

Wafers: HBM rises to nearly 30 per cent of DRAM wafer input in 2027 and takes 3 to 4x the wafers per bit. 

Conventional DRAM gets squeezed.
CPUs: NVDA says agentic AI demand for CPUs is “far outstripping supply” and sees CPU revenue more than doubling.

GPUs: a three-year-old H100 rents for $ 3.07 an hour, up 54 per cent in a year. CoreWeave has 10x more demand than capacity through 2027, and 2028 is already several times capacity.

Capex: cloud spending is up another 60 per cent in 2027, to about $ 1.5 trillion.

If demand were fading, old chips would get cheaper. They are getting dearer.

AI demand is strong. Ignore the doomers.

DRAM:
• Contract prices started climbing in 3Q25 and were up ~45% QoQ by 4Q25
• 1Q26 was the peak: blended ASP roughly doubled in one quarter, with PC DDR5 up ~110%
• 2Q26 added another ~60%, led by server DDR4 at ~70%

NAND:
• Later and a bit smaller: ~+30% in 4Q25, ~+57% in 1Q26, ~+75% in 2Q26
• Enterprise SSD led both quarters at ~+80%

What's forecast next:
• 3Q26: DRAM ~+15%, NAND ~+20%
• 4Q26: both around +10%
• 2027: DRAM flattens to low single digits, while NAND turns negative from 2Q27 and is falling 10–15% QoQ by 4Q27

Financing cancellations mean less future competition, good for $NBIS long-term as well-capitalized neoclouds with hyperscaler counterparties win; macro risks like rates impact neoclouds most.
text:
Of course! uhh two things: 

1. Asian neoclouds (eg. Malaysia/Thailand) had their deals cancelled with Bytedance, Tencent etc. due to US export controls. 

So they'll reroute spare capacity back to US players. 

Many are arguing that creates compute flooding, but $CRWV cited 10x demand > supply entering 2027. 

So even if supply comes in, I would still see a large demand imbalance, not prices crashing. If anything... pricing has still gone up from some trackers. But we'll see the full effects in the incoming weeks. 

2. Asian Neoclouds had their financing cancelled/paused due to ongoing risks. 

This is more nuanced, it means less compute/competition comes online in the future, which is a good thing for players like $NBIS? 

It might hurt some semi supply chains (not US neoclouds) as seen with some spot prices dropping around GPU/DRAM  procurement. 

But China would need to build out their own compute anyway for their frontier labs so I see a primarily shift in order timing + bifurcated supply chains than aggregate demand falling. 

I see the well capitalized Neoclouds (with hyperscaler counterparties) winning in the long run like $NBIS, but as Elon said with the "other gupplies" there might be some trouble. 

There's still the overall macro risks like rate hikes, financing, etc. where Neoclouds are typically the most impacted

DOES A $VIX SPIKE MEAN BUY? THE ACADEMIC EVIDENCE, THE REBUTTALS, AND A CONCLUSION

THE CLAIM

The folk version says buy when the fear gauge screams. The academic version is narrower and more interesting: expected equity returns step up, nonlinearly, after implied volatility reaches extreme levels, and the step-up is large enough to measure years of data at a time. Both versions circulate every time the VIX prints 30 or 35. They are not the same claim, and the literature supports them very differently.

• Ronn and Xu (Econometrics, 2025) test the folk version directly. Across 29 historical episodes in which the VIX exceeded 30, a strategy of cutting equity exposure above 30 and buying back when volatility subsided underperformed simply holding through the episodes by 10.9% a year. Subsequent S&P 500 returns rose with the level of the VIX. Their conclusion for investors with a high appetite for risk: when the VIX is high, invest, because on average you will be compensated.

🚨 This is one of the craziest things I’ve seen all year.

A newly public Google patent filing describes a TV channel that could generate shows for an audience of one. 

It could even cast you as the lead, with a character who looks like you and speaks in your voice. 

Google calls the concept “My Channel.” Open it and you’d see a lineup of titles and descriptions, much like any streaming app. 

The difference is where those titles come from. Google’s system would use your viewing history, language, location and age group to write prompts for AI to create videos specifically for you. 

Say you watch a lot of crime thrillers and comedies. 

Your channel could offer a crime comedy with you playing the detective. In one version of the design, the system would build your character from your photos and use a synthetic version of your voice to deliver the lines. 

The detail that caught my attention as a $GOOGL investor is that advertising is already in the design. 

The filing describes a system that could stitch targeted ads into the video before playback. Think about what that would mean for two people turning on their TVs at the same time. 

They could each get a different show, with a different lead character and a different advertiser. 

Things are about to get crazy.

To the status quo growth is bad. 

Holtz-Eakin is reading the wrong gauge, and the Fed shouldn’t follow him.

Nominal GDP is not a measure of overheating. It counts output and prices together. Third-quarter nominal growth was 6.2%, and 4.3 points of that was real output . Prices contributed about 1.9 points, which is target-consistent. Calling that “excessively demand-driven” misreads the arithmetic.

His argument also has no place for productivity. With GDP revised up, Q3 productivity is heading from 3.6% to 4.8% annualised. Hours barely moved, so the output is coming from each worker producing more. Unit labour costs were already falling, and that revision pushes them lower. Overheated demand does the opposite.

“Core inflation has never come close to 2%” is no case for a 50 basis point hike. The energy shock that has inflated prices will dissipate by spring, when the base effects roll off and PCE returns toward 2%. A hike cannot produce a barrel of oil. It would tighten against a price shock that is already ending, and a Fed that hikes to “send a message” is substituting posture for policy.

The cost of that message is large. A 50 basis point move would put the real funds rate above neutral and tighter than Greenspan’s in 1995, just as the productivity gains he bet on appear in the data. A Fed that cannot tell a supply boom from a demand boom should not set rates.

Seeing some of these previously credible companies abuse ATM offerings had me thinking...

On a decade-long timeframe, some of X's favorite small and mid cap names will cease to exist.

The "safest" stocks you can own would be names like $GOOGL, $META, $NVDA, $SPCX, and a few more.

Sounds odd after the month we just had, but volatility isn't the risk on a longer timeframe...

The real risk is that a lot of these smaller names won't compound, have dilution mismanagement, or will get acquired for pieces.

This absolutely does not mean they can't be multi-bagger momentum trades on a shorter timeframe.

You just need to understand your own approach... what timeline you're investing on, and which basket each position belongs to.

I think it's particularly important to have a barbell approach, where a portion of your portfolio compounds slowly but stably... and another portion is left for asymmetric opportunities.

If there's a 10% chance you can get a 10x trade, you should probably take it... every single time.

But full-porting either extreme is not the way to go.

Just some shower thoughts!

Happy Thanksgiving, my friends 🫂

"I didn't say all companies should. I said that most companies should. And people should also get into the hygiene of considering it regularly."

"And so Ben Horowitz I think wrote a blog post about this maybe, I don't know what, ten years ago, fifteen years ago, a long time ago. Which is basically a good corporate hygiene mechanism for a startup is once a year have a pre planned board meeting where you talk about selling the company. And that doesn't mean you will. It just takes all the emotion out of it. It's not the founders wanting to sell. It's not the VCs or investors or board members pushing for it.
